best_for: Developers on Windows who juggle PowerShell, WSL and SSH sessions and want them in one tabbed window with a saved connection list.
description:
Tabby, once called Terminus, is a free terminal app, SSH client and serial client, open source under the MIT license. Its developers pitch it as a stand-in for the standard Windows console, PowerShell ISE, PuTTY, macOS Terminal and iTerm.

You can send files to and from an SSH session with Zmodem, get proper tab completion in Windows shells through Clink, and turn on font ligatures. Tabby can tell you when a long command finishes, warns before you paste several lines at once, and lets you put tabs on any side of the window. Plugins, such as one for Docker containers, install from the Settings screen. Its SSH, SFTP and Telnet client also runs as a web app you can host yourself.

points.title: Terminal plus SSH and serial
points.text: Tabby has built-in SSH2, Telnet and serial clients. SSH covers port and X11 forwarding, jump hosts, agent forwarding including Pageant, and login scripts. Serial sessions get hex input and auto reconnect.

points.title: Every Windows shell in one place
points.text: It runs PowerShell, CMD, WSL, Git Bash, Cygwin, MSYS2 and Cmder in tabs and split panes. A dropdown Quake-style console is also available.

points.title: Secrets in an encrypted vault
points.text: SSH passwords and keys can sit in an integrated encrypted container instead of plain config files.

points.title: Heavy on memory
points.text: The project says plainly it is not lightweight, and points readers who care about RAM use to ConEmu or Alacritty instead.

points.title: No built-in config sync
points.text: Settings do not sync between machines out of the box. A community plugin can sync them to a Gist or Gitee. Tabby is free under the MIT license with no account.

points.title: Portable on Windows
points.text: Create a `data` folder next to `Tabby.exe` and it runs as a portable app. Installers come for x64 and Arm64, per user or per machine.

points.title: Mac and Linux get less history here
points.text: The Windows listing keeps 86 versions; macOS lists only the current release, for Intel and Apple Silicon on macOS 12 or later. Linux packages (deb, rpm, pacman) come from the project's GitHub releases.
